subject: [PATCH 05/46] mm/truncate: look again if a folio left the mapping

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary: Reviewer questioned the necessity of an additional lookup when the last batch reaches the end, suggesting that the code is simpler and more consistent if it exits without another look.
reviews.raw_body:
But that's then another lookup even if not really required?

Why do you thing that is that better?

I agree that the code is simpler, but at least it's consistent with the other
handling.

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
reviews.summary: Author acknowledged a concern about an extra lookup in the second loop, explained that it's only necessary when the first pass didn't remove everything, and agreed to leave the choice of implementation up to the reviewer.
reviews.raw_body:
The extra lookup only happens when the second loop had work to do.
Normally the first pass removes everything, the first lookup from start
comes back empty, and both versions stop there. When the second loop did
run to end, it costs one more lookup over a range that is now empty.

What I like about it is one way to look again instead of two: the loop
already goes back to start when the last batch ends below end, and the
patch adds a second way for when it ends at end. truncate is not like
shmem here: shmem_undo_range() stops after one sweep on hole punch on
purpose, so it needs the rewind; truncate was meant to sweep until
nothing is left.

Your version fixes the bug too, so I'll leave the choice to you.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary: Reviewer David suggested a simpler alternative to the original patch, replacing the condition `index <= end` with `start >= end`, and providing an inline review of specific code changes.

2026-10-29.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the truncate operation in the Linux kernel by reducing the number of lookups required when a folio is left behind in the mapping. Normally, two lookups are performed: one from the start and one from the end of the range. However, if the second loop had work to do, it means that there's still something left in the mapping, so instead of performing another lookup from the start, the patch reuses the existing loop that goes back to the start when necessary. This reduces the number of lookups required and improves performance.
